newsitem.title: CHINA: China seen hard pressed to create new jobs.
newsitem.headline: China seen hard pressed to create new jobs.

text.p: China will be hard pressed to find jobs for about 175 million farmers and workers who will be laid off or made redundant in the transition to a market-style economy, officials said on Tuesday.
Some 137 million farmers would move to other sectors in the five years from 1996-2000, said Wang Dongjin, a vice-minister of the State Commission for Restructuring the Economic System.
Beijing had resolved to expand experiments with bankruptcies and mergers, putting pressure on the job market as more workers became redundant, Wang told reporters.
"It will be an arduous task for us to find jobs for these people," Wang said.
About 54 million urban workers would be forced to find other jobs but even China's breakneck economy would be able to create only 38 million new jobs in that time, Wang said.
"The main way to resolve the unemployment problem is to further develop our economy so as to produce more employment opportunities," he said.

Other officials have estimated that 130 million farmers would move out of the agricultural sector in the five years to 2000 and more than 14 million urban workers would be seeking jobs after being laid off from companies trying to streamline.
Some officials have estimated China's jobless rate could climb as high as 7.4 percent by the year 2000, but Wang said Beijing wanted to control this to within four percent.
Official figures show an urban unemployment rate of 3.0 percent in 1996.

Wang said private, foreign-funded and small-scale individual or family businesses had absorbed 60 percent of the work force while the state sector now accounted for just 30 percent, about half the previous figure.

Lay-offs from bankrupt or merged state-owned enterprises would leave 15-20 million people jobless, Wang said, adding that Beijing would try to help workers find new jobs instead of continuing to pay unemployment benefits.
"The problem of redundant employees of state-owned enterprises, and their historical and social burdens...has not been fundamentally resolved," said Hong Hu, also a vice-minister of the commission.

While the number of bankruptcies in China has increased in recent years, Beijing has shied away from widespread use of the practice out of fears of creating a huge and disgruntled pool of urban jobless.
"Bankruptcies can cause quite a large social disturbance," Hong said. "Workers in those bankrupt enterprises may not be prepared psychologically."

China was expanding the number of cities allowed to handle bankruptcies to 111 in 1997 from 58 last year and had earmarked 30 billion yuan ($3.6 billion) of reserve funds to help clear bad debts of state firms, Hong said.
China last month set up a new body to handle bankruptcies and mergers and help the jobless in a major step toward reforming the lumbering state sector.

A total of 6,232 firms declared bankruptcy in 1996 compared with 5,395 between 1989 and 1995, but the figure is just a fraction of China's estimated 10 million companies, of which some 100,000 are state-owned.
